questions.q: What is 'alert fatigue', as this lesson defines it?
options: The point at which a team starts ignoring alerts because too many have been low-value or false
A hardware condition where a server's CPU overheats
A SQL Server licensing restriction on the number of alerts allowed
The time it takes for an alert to actually reach a responder
questions.explain: Alert fatigue is a human/organizational problem — too much noise causes real alerts to get tuned out.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend deriving alert thresholds from a server's own real baseline data instead of a generic guessed number?
options: A server's normal behavior varies — a generic threshold like '80% CPU' may fire constantly during expected, normal workload spikes on a busy server
Baseline data is required by SQL Server licensing for any threshold to be valid
Generic numbers are always too high and never fire at all
PowerShell cannot evaluate a numeric comparison without baseline data
questions.explain: The lesson's CPU example shows a server that normally runs at 85% during batch windows — a flat 80% threshold would fire on completely expected behavior.

questions.q: What does the lesson's alert-suppression example track before sending a new notification?
options: Whether an alert for the same specific condition already fired recently, within a defined time window
The total number of SQL Server instances in the environment
The DBA's current on-call schedule
Whether the ticketing system is currently online
questions.explain: The suppression pattern checks a state file keyed by the specific alert condition and a recent timestamp before firing again.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about escalating on a single blip versus a real pattern?
options: Escalation should wait for a condition to recur across several checks or persist meaningfully, rather than treating one sample as equally urgent as a sustained problem
Every single sample above a threshold should escalate immediately, with no exceptions
Escalation should never happen automatically, only manually
A single blip should always be escalated to the highest urgency level available
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly favors requiring a real pattern — recurrence or duration — before escalating, since a single blip is often just noise.

questions.q: This lesson closes Chapter Six. What does the outro tease for Lesson 33?
options: What DevOps actually changes for a DBA, opening Chapter Seven
A capstone project combining all prior chapters
Another lesson on incident creation APIs
A return to Infrastructure as Code topics
questions.explain: Lesson 33, "What DevOps Actually Changes for a DBA," opens Chapter Seven: DevOps Culture for DBAs.
